# Put a web service under load {#sec-lab-03 .unnumbered}

*Exercise 3 · Session 3 lab · Estimated time: 75-100 min*

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
This is the practical task for [Chapter 3: Web services, load and denial of service](../chapters/03-web-services-load-dos.qmd).
Work through it in your lab group; you talk your answers through at the
session after next (the review runs one session behind). **This page
mirrors the worksheet for reading and reference - the official worksheet
is the PDF distributed via Canvas.**
:::

Write your answers in the answer document `SKY2100_Exercise3_Answers.docx`. Today you stand up a real web server, attack it with
*controlled* load, and read what the metrics and logs show. You will watch a service degrade
gracefully and then hit the wall - the same shape whether the load is real customers or a
denial-of-service attack. This is your first hands-on encounter with the **Availability** leg of
the CIA triad.

::: {.callout-warning}
Run load *against your own VM only* (`localhost`). Pointing a load generator at a
machine or site you do not own is an attack, and it is illegal.
:::

## Stand up a web server

- [ ] **Install Nginx and the benchmark tool:** `sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y nginx apache2-utils`. Open `http://localhost/` in the VM browser and confirm the welcome page loads.

## Generate and watch load

- [ ] **Watch the system:** in terminal 1 run `htop` (or `btop`); keep it visible.
- [ ] **Generate load** (terminal 2): `ab -n 2000 -c 100 http://localhost/`. Record in the answer
  document: requests per second, time per request (mean), failed requests.
- [ ] **Increase the pressure:** repeat with `ab -n 5000 -c 300 http://localhost/`. Note at roughly how
  many concurrent requests response time climbs sharply.
- [ ] **Read the logs:** `sudo tail -n 20 /var/log/nginx/access.log`; correlate the burst of log
  lines with the spike you saw in `htop`.

::: {.callout-tip title="Aha"}
Watch what happened as you raised the concurrency. Requests per second climbed for a while, then
flattened, and past a certain point response times shot up and requests began to fail. That is your
VM meeting its capacity ceiling, and the shape of the curve is the same whether the load is real
customers on a launch day or an attacker sending a flood. This is why availability is a security
property, not just an operations concern: a denial-of-service attack does nothing clever, it simply
pushes you past the point you just found. Note the concurrency where your own server broke, because
every defence later in the course, from rate limiting to autoscaling, is about moving that point or
soaking up load before it arrives.
:::

- [ ] **Interpret your run in 2-3 sentences: what happened to CPU/RAM and requests-per-second as
  concurrency rose?**

## Optional stretch - a first control

Add a rate limit (`limit_req_zone` / `limit_req`), reload Nginx, re-run the high-concurrency
test, and compare the failed-request count before/after.

## Knowledge check

1.  A DDoS attack primarily targets which CIA property?
    a) ☐ Confidentiality
    b) ☐ Integrity
    c) ☐ Availability

    *Hint: It floods the service offline - which of the three properties is that?*

2.  Name the three flavours of DDoS and give one example of each.

    *Hint: By raw volume, by protocol tricks, and at the application layer.*

3.  `ab -n 1000 -c 50` means…
    a) ☐ 1000 concurrent requests
    b) ☐ 1000 requests total, 50 at a time
    c) ☐ 50 requests total
    d) ☐ 1000 servers

    *Hint: A thousand requests in total, fifty running at a time.*

4.  Why is an **application-layer** DDoS the hardest to tell apart from legitimate traffic?

    *Hint: Its requests are valid and, one by one, indistinguishable from real users.*

5.  An Azure **Application Gateway** operates at which layer, and which security control does it
    host?

    *Hint: Layer 7 - and it is where the WAF lives.*

6.  What is a **composite SLA**, and why can adding services *lower* overall availability?

    *Hint: Chained services multiply their availabilities, so the combined figure drops.*

7.  List *two* controls on your own server and *two* that work only at cloud scale,
    against DDoS.

    *Hint: Local: rate limits, caching, timeouts. Cloud: autoscaling, CDN, DDoS protection.*

8.  Define **capacity** and **availability**, and state the relationship between them.

    *Hint: One is work per second the system can do; one is being reachable when needed.*

9.  According to Comer (Ch. 1), what early problem led to clusters of servers behind a load
    balancer?

    *Hint: Early sites outgrew a single machine, so many ran behind a balancer.*

10. Distinguish **scale-up** from **scale-out**, and say which the cloud favours.

    *Hint: A bigger single box versus more boxes - the cloud prefers more.*

11. Multi-tenancy + autoscaling produces a "moving attack surface". Explain in one sentence why
    that complicates security.

    *Hint: Instances come and go and tenants share hardware - there is no fixed list to guard.*

12. (Reflection - from your data) At what concurrency did response time climb sharply, and what does
    that tell you about *your* VM's capacity?

## Solutions {.unnumbered}

*Work through the lab first, then check here. Model answers are indicative - equivalent reasoning is fine.*

**Note:** Model answers are indicative - accept equivalent reasoning. Multiple-choice
answers are in **bold**.

### Knowledge check

1.  **Availability.**
2.  **Volumetric** (UDP flood / amplification), **Protocol** (SYN flood),
    **Application-layer** (HTTP flood of an expensive endpoint).
3.  **1000 requests total, 50 at a time.**
4.  It uses small, valid-looking requests, individually indistinguishable from real users; only
    aggregate behaviour and logs reveal it.
5.  **Layer 7** (application layer); it hosts the **WAF**.
6.  A **composite SLA** is the combined SLA of chained services; multiplying availabilities
    (e.g. $0.9995\times0.9995$) yields a *lower* number than any component - so more
    components means lower combined availability.
7.  Local: rate limiting, caching, timeouts and connection limits. Cloud-scale: autoscaling,
    CDN/anycast, cloud DDoS protection, WAF.
8.  **Capacity** = work per unit time a system can do; **Availability** = reachable/
    responsive when needed; availability fails once demand exceeds capacity.
9.  Popular early web sites exceeded a single machine's capacity, so operators ran a *cluster*
    of identical servers behind a load balancer. (Comer Ch. 1.5, p. 8, verified.)
10. **Scale-up** = a bigger single machine; **scale-out** = more machines. The cloud
    favours **scale-out**.
11. Instances appear/disappear and tenants share hardware, so you cannot secure a fixed list of
    servers - only a pattern/policy; the surface changes continuously.
12. Reflection from each group's own measurement - no fixed value.
